docs.title: Small board. Big ideas.
docs.text:
What could you make with two buttons, a display and a few lines of code? In this unit, you will turn a BBC micro:bit into a pocket character, a dice, a treasure alarm and a wireless messaging system.

You will learn programming concepts using Microsoft MakeCode Blocks, with micro:bit examples that show how each idea works. Your teacher will guide you through the concept pages and the matching tasks in your workbook. You will predict what your code will do, try it in the simulator, test it on a real micro:bit and improve it using evidence from your tests.

Your final mission brings these skills together: design, build and improve a classroom help system that lets a pupil request help and a teacher acknowledge the request.

docs.title: Learn a concept, then apply it
docs.text:
Start with the Teaching lessons section for explanations, diagrams and worked examples. Each numbered teaching page links the concept to a micro:bit example and a workbook activity. Revisit earlier programs as you learn new ideas. The practical reference guides retain their original project numbers.

Sequence, selection and iteration are the three core constructs. The other concept pages explain the data, events and communication that help you build complete programs.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
By the end of the unit, you will be able to:

  • Explain how inputs, processing and outputs work together in a physical computing system.
  • Use events, sequences and loops to control what a program does and when it runs.
  • Store information in variables and use selection to make decisions.
  • Work with sensor readings, random numbers, coordinates and ordered sequences.
  • Send and receive radio messages between two micro:bits.
  • Use functions to organise and reuse code.
  • Test a program against its requirements, find faults and explain your improvements.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You will need:

  • A computer with access to Microsoft MakeCode for micro:bit.
  • A BBC micro:bit and a USB data cable for downloading and testing your programs.
  • Your workbook to record designs, code screenshots, test results and explanations.
  • A partner and two powered micro:bits for the radio missions.

Use the Blocks editor throughout the unit. Some missions use a starter program or framework; follow your teacher's instructions to access it.

Build, test, improve

Predict the result before running your code. Compare what actually happens with what you expected. If something goes wrong, record the fault, make a change and test again.

docs.title: Make your progress visible
docs.text:
For every mission, save your project using the name given in the lesson and download a .hex backup. Add readable screenshots to your workbook, record actual test results and answer the questions in your own words. When working with a partner, both of you should be able to explain how the code works.

Keep your micro:bit close to the desk and handle its cable carefully. For radio tasks, use your teacher's allocated group so your messages reach the intended boards.

Start with Lesson 1: Inputs, events and sequence.

docs.title: Project reference 01: Pocket personality
docs.text:
Learning intention: Program a character that reacts to buttons using inputs, events and sequence.

Key ideas: Events; sequence; inputs; processing; outputs

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 1: Inputs, events and sequence

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Start your project
docs.text:
1. Open MakeCode for micro:bit and choose New Project. Name it S1-01-Personality. Stay in Blocks.
  2. Keep on start. Remove the empty forever block by dragging it back into the toolbox.
  3. From Basic, put show icon inside on start. Choose a heart. The start event runs when the program starts or the board resets.

docs.title: Task 2: Create two button sequences
docs.text:
1. From Input, add on button A pressed. Inside it, show a happy face, pause 500 ms, then show a heart.
  2. Add another button event and select B. Inside it, show a sad face, pause 500 ms, then show a diamond.
  3. Predict the image order for each button, then test in the simulator.
  4. Swap the two images in one event. Predict and test the difference, then restore your chosen order.

docs.title: Task 3: Use the real micro:bit
docs.text:
1. Connect the board with a USB data cable. Follow the download instructions in the Getting Started guide.
  2. Try each button separately. Wait for its sequence to finish before trying the other button.
  3. Change the startup icon and the two button reactions to suit your character. Keep both button events.
  4. Save your project and download a backup .hex file. Complete workbook lesson 1.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Reset the board Your chosen startup icon appears. Press A Happy face, pause, then heart. Press B Sad face, pause, then diamond.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: All three event blocks: startup and both complete button sequences.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. Name two inputs and one output in this program.
  2. What is an event? Give an example from your code.
  3. Why does the order of images and pauses inside a button event matter?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: Add an A+B event that shows your character name. Test it after the other animations finish.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Save the named project and a .hex backup.
  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 02: The unfair dice challenge
docs.text:
Learning intention: Find a faulty dice rule and build a dice with six equally possible outcomes.

Key ideas: Variables; random numbers; selection; debugging

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 2: Variables and random numbers
  • Lesson 3: Selection and comparisons

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Investigate a faulty dice
docs.text:
1. Create S1-02-Dice. From Variables, make a variable called roll.
  2. In on shake, set roll to pick random 1 to 6. Find pick random in Math.
  3. Below that, add if then from Logic. Set its condition to roll = 6. Inside it, set roll to 1.
  4. After the if, add show number roll. Predict which number can never appear and which has an extra chance.
  5. Shake the simulator repeatedly. Explain the fault before removing anything. Take a screenshot of this faulty version.

docs.title: Task 2: Repair the rule
docs.text:
1. Delete the whole if block, leaving set roll to pick random 1 to 6, followed by show number roll.
  2. Download and try the corrected program. Wait for each roll to finish before shaking again.
  3. Make a tally for 30 rolls in your workbook. Record every result, including repeated results.
  4. Check that no result is below 1 or above 6. You do not need all six tallies to be equal.

docs.title: Task 3: Explain and save
docs.text:
1. Use the variable roll in your explanation: it stores the chosen number until it is changed.
  2. Explain why 30 rolls cannot prove that a dice is fair.
  3. Save the corrected project and backup .hex. Add a second screenshot showing the repaired code.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Read the faulty rule A roll of 6 is changed to 1; 6 cannot be displayed. Inspect corrected random limits Lower limit is 1; upper limit is 6. Carry out 30 corrected rolls Every result is an integer from 1 to 6. Add all six tally counts The total is 30.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: Faulty dice program before the repair.
  • Screenshot: Corrected dice program.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. Explain why the faulty version favours 1.
  2. What information does roll store?
  3. Why might a fair dice show more 4s than 2s in 30 rolls?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: Add on button A pressed to show the previous roll without generating a new one.

docs.text:

  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 03: Beat the reaction timer
docs.text:
Learning intention: Measure a reaction time and detect an early press.

Key ideas: State; multiple variables; selection; time calculations

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Selection and comparisons
  • Boolean logic and state

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Load the starter
docs.text:
1. Create S1-03-Reaction. Your teacher supplies 03-reaction-starter.ts. Follow the JavaScript-to-Blocks steps in Getting Started.
  2. Read the starter: B begins a round; phase is 0 when idle, 1 while waiting, and 2 when the signal is showing.
  3. The starter already waits a random 1000 to 3000 ms. Do not change its B event yet.

docs.title: Task 2: Finish the A event
docs.text:
1. Add on button A pressed. Inside it, add if / else if from Logic using the small plus button on the if block.
  2. First condition: phase = 1. Inside, set phase to 0, then show string EARLY.
  3. Second condition: phase = 2. Inside, set reactionTime to running time (ms) minus startTime. Find running time under Input, more.
  4. Still inside the second branch, set phase to 0, then show number reactionTime.
  5. Leave out an else branch. A should do nothing when phase is 0.

docs.title: Task 3: Test the timer
docs.text:
1. Press B, wait for the diamond, then press A. The displayed value is your time in milliseconds.
  2. Start another round. Press A before the diamond: EARLY should appear and the round should stop.
  3. Complete five valid attempts in your workbook. Restart only after a result or message finishes.
  4. Keep the board on the desk so everyone has the same starting setup. Save and screenshot all event blocks.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Press A before starting No reaction time is displayed. Press B, wait for diamond, press A A non-negative reaction time in ms appears. Press B then press A before signal EARLY appears; no later diamond starts that round. Press B again during waiting The existing round continues; no extra round starts.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: All event blocks and startup variables. Split into two readable images if necessary.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. What do phase values 0, 1 and 2 mean?
  2. Why calculate running time minus startTime?
  3. Why use a random waiting time?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: Add bestTime, starting at 99999. Update it only when a valid reactionTime is smaller. Show it with A+B.

docs.text:

  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 04: Protect the treasure
docs.text:
Learning intention: Use a measured light threshold to trigger an armed alarm.

Key ideas: Real-world input; thresholds; Boolean variables; repetition

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 4: Iteration
  • Lesson 5: Boolean logic and state

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Measure the light
docs.text:
1. Create S1-04-Alarm. Add on button A+B pressed containing show number light level. Find light level in Input.
  2. Download. Cover the front LED display with your hand, press A+B and record the reading. Uncover it and repeat.
  3. The display also senses light. Use a threshold between your covered and uncovered readings. Do not assume everyone needs the same number.

docs.title: Task 2: Set up the alarm
docs.text:
1. Create variables armed, triggered and threshold. In on start, set armed to false, triggered to false and threshold to your chosen number. Find true and false in Logic.
  2. In on button A pressed: clear screen, set triggered to false, then set armed to true.
  3. In on button B pressed: set armed to false, set triggered to false, then clear screen.
  4. In forever, add if armed AND light level > threshold then set triggered to true. Build AND using Logic.

docs.title: Task 3: Make a warning that stays on
docs.text:
1. Below that if, still inside forever, add another if: armed AND triggered.
  2. Inside, show icon No (cross), pause 200 ms, clear screen, pause 200 ms.
  3. This is a visual alarm. No speaker is required. It keeps flashing even if the light level drops again.
  4. Cover the board before pressing A to arm it, then uncover it. B must stop the alarm. Leave the A+B light reader for calibration while disarmed.
  5. Save, test and record your threshold and readings in the workbook.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Disarmed; expose display to light No flashing alarm. Cover display, then press A Board arms without triggering if reading is below threshold. Uncover armed board Warning starts flashing. Cover again after triggering Warning continues. Press B while flashing Alarm stops within one flash cycle, allowing for an in-progress pause.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: All event blocks and the complete forever loop.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. What is a threshold?
  2. Why does triggered stay true after the board is covered again?
  3. Explain the input, processing and output.

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: After testing, choose a different threshold and record one example of a false alarm or missed opening.

docs.text:
• Save the named project and a .hex backup.
  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 05: Tilt arcade
docs.text:
Learning intention: Move a dot safely across the display by tilting the board.

Key ideas: Coordinates; boundaries; variables; named functions

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 6: Coordinates and boundaries
  • Lesson 7: Functions

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Create the game
docs.text:
1. Create S1-05-Tilt. Make variables x, targetX, score and playing.
  2. Open Advanced > Functions. Make a function called resetGame with no extra input spaces.
  3. Inside it: set x to 2; set targetX to 4; set score to 0; set playing to true; clear screen.
  4. In on start, call resetGame. In on button A pressed, also call resetGame. The same instructions are reused.

docs.title: Task 2: Draw and move the player
docs.text:
1. In forever, add if playing. Put all the following game instructions inside it.
  2. Clear screen. Plot x, 4 using Led > plot x y. Plot targetX, 0. Coordinates run from 0 to 4; x is across and y is down.
  3. Add if acceleration (mg) x < -300 AND x > 0: change x by -1.
  4. Below it add a separate if acceleration (mg) x > 300 AND x < 4: change x by 1. Find acceleration in Input.
  5. Add pause 200 ms at the end of the if playing block. Tilt gently; keep the board near the desk.

docs.title: Task 3: Score a hit
docs.text:
1. Add on button B pressed. Inside, add if playing AND x = targetX.
  2. Inside: change score by 1; set playing to false; show number score; set targetX to pick random 0 to 4; set x to 2; set playing to true.
  3. B scores only when the player is in the target column. A resets the whole game.
  4. Test both edges repeatedly. Save and screenshot the function and all events.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Press A Player returns to centre; score is 0; target is column 4. Tilt left for several seconds Player stops at column 0. Tilt right for several seconds Player stops at column 4. Press B in wrong column Score does not increase. Press B aligned with target Score increases by 1; a new target is selected.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: resetGame function.
  • Screenshot: Startup, forever and both button events.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. Why check x > 0 before moving left?
  2. What is the difference between defining and calling resetGame?
  3. How do the forever loop and button event share information?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: Add a lives variable starting at 3. A wrong B press loses one life; at 0 set playing to false and show a cross.

docs.text:

  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 06: Memory master
docs.text:
Learning intention: Store and check an ordered sequence of button choices.

Key ideas: Lists; indexes; iteration; selection; subprograms

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 8: Lists and indexing

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Read the supplied framework
docs.text:
1. Create S1-06-Memory. Load 06-memory-starter.ts as explained in Getting Started, then return to Blocks.
  2. The sequence list contains 0, 1, 0. In this game, 0 means A and 1 means B.
  3. The list positions are 0, 1 and 2. The first item is at index 0, not index 1.
  4. Find the playSequence function. It shows each item as A or B, then sets accepting to true. A+B calls this function.

docs.title: Task 2: Finish the checking function
docs.text:
1. Find the empty function checkChoice. Keep its supplied choice block. The A event will use 0 in the call block and the B event will use 1; use choice in the comparison below.
  2. Inside it add if accepting. All checking instructions go inside this condition.
  3. Inside, add if choice = sequence get value at index position. Find list get value at in Advanced > Arrays. Drag the sequence variable into the list socket.
  4. In the correct branch, change position by 1. Then add if position = length of array sequence. Inside that, set accepting to false and show icon Yes (tick).
  5. In the wrong branch, set accepting to false and show icon No (cross).

docs.title: Task 3: Connect the buttons and test
docs.text:
1. In on button A pressed, call checkChoice with 0. In on button B pressed, call checkChoice with 1.
  2. Press A+B, watch the sequence finish, then enter A, B, A. You should get a tick.
  3. Start again. Deliberately give a wrong answer. You should get a cross.
  4. Change the list in on start to 1, 0, 1, 1. Replay it and test B, A, B, B. The same checker should work without changing a hard-coded length.
  5. Save and screenshot both the list setup and the complete checking function.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Press A before playback No answer is accepted. Play [0,1,0], enter A,B,A Tick after the third correct answer. Play [0,1,0], enter B first Cross; further answers ignored. Change list to [1,0,1,1], enter B,A,B,B Tick after the fourth answer. Press A+B after finishing Position resets and the sequence plays again.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: Startup list, button events and playSequence.
  • Screenshot: Complete checkChoice function.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. What is stored at index 1 in [0,1,0]?
  2. Why is a list better than three separate variables here?
  3. Why compare position with the list length?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: At the start of playSequence, replace the list with three random values from 0 to 1. Keep the checking function unchanged.

docs.text:
• Save the named project and a .hex backup.
  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 07: Wireless rescue team
docs.text:
Learning intention: Send a help message and receive an acknowledgement between two boards.

Key ideas: Sender; receiver; messages; communicating processes

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 9: Radio communication

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Prepare two projects
docs.text:
1. Work with another pupil so there are two boards. Label them FIELD and BASE. Keep both connected to computers if you have no battery packs.
  2. Your teacher allocates a radio group from 1 to 255. Both your boards use the same group. Other teams use different groups.
  3. Create S1-07-Field and S1-07-Base as separate projects. In each on start, add Radio > radio set group with your allocated number.
  4. A radio group filters traffic; it is not a password, private channel or individual device address.

docs.title: Task 2: Build FIELD
docs.text:
1. In FIELD, on button A pressed: radio send string HELP, then show icon Question.
  2. Add on radio received receivedString. Inside, if receivedString = OK, show icon Yes. Text must match exactly, including capitals.

docs.title: Task 3: Build BASE
docs.text:
1. In BASE, add on radio received receivedString. Inside, if receivedString = HELP, show string H.
  2. In on button B pressed: radio send string OK, then clear screen.
  3. Download each project to the correctly labelled board. Test A on FIELD, then B on BASE.
  4. Swap who operates each board and repeat. Draw the message journey in the workbook. Save both projects and add both code screenshots.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Both boards use same group; FIELD A FIELD shows question mark; BASE shows H. BASE B after request BASE clears; FIELD shows tick. Temporarily change BASE to a different group and download A new FIELD request is not received by BASE. Restore matching group and download Communication works again.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: Complete FIELD program.
  • Screenshot: Complete BASE program.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. Which board sends and which receives? Can a board do both?
  2. Do two forever loops on different boards automatically communicate?
  3. What does the radio group do?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: FIELD A+B sends CHECK. BASE displays C on receiving CHECK. Keep HELP and OK working.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Save the named project and a .hex backup.
  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 08: Secret signals laboratory
docs.text:
Learning intention: Encode a numeric message with a shared key and explain its limitations.

Key ideas: Representation; simple encryption; variables; communication

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Variables and random numbers
  • Radio communication

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Agree the message meaning
docs.text:
1. Use two boards and one allocated radio group. Create S1-08-Sender and S1-08-Receiver.
  2. Agree this codebook: 1 = need help; 2 = task finished; 3 = please check. Writing a meaning as a number is encoding, not encryption.
  3. In both programs, make a variable key and set it to 7 in on start. Also set the same radio group in both.

docs.title: Task 2: Build SENDER
docs.text:
1. Create a variable message and set it to 1 in on start.
  2. On button A pressed: change message by 1; if message > 3 then set message to 1; show number message.
  3. On button B pressed: radio send number message + key, then show icon Yes.
  4. Use A to choose a message and B to send it.

docs.title: Task 3: Build RECEIVER
docs.text:
1. Create a variable decoded. Add on radio received receivedNumber. This is the NUMBER event, not the string event.
  2. Inside: set decoded to receivedNumber - key. Then show number decoded. Use the codebook to interpret it.
  3. Send all three messages. Record the original value, transmitted value and decoded value in the workbook.
  4. Temporarily change RECEIVER key to 6. Send message 2. Record the incorrect result, then restore key 7.
  5. Another pair is told that the transmitted value was 9 and the original was 2. Ask them to find the key. Save and screenshot both programs.

docs.title: Task 4: Explain the security
docs.text:
1. The add/subtract rule is a toy encryption model for learning. It is very easy to break and must not protect real secrets.
  2. A group number does not hide message contents. An observer using the same group can receive the transmitted number.
  3. Discuss how knowing one original/transmitted pair reveals this key.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Send 1 with key 7 Transmitted 8; receiver displays 1. Send 2 with key 7 Transmitted 9; receiver displays 2. Send 3 with key 7 Transmitted 10; receiver displays 3. Sender key 7; receiver key 6; send 2 Receiver displays 3, showing the wrong meaning. Restore both keys to 7 Original meaning is recovered.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: Complete SENDER program.
  • Screenshot: Complete RECEIVER program.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. What is the difference between the codebook and the shared key?
  2. How can someone find the key if 2 is transmitted as 9?
  3. Could the number 1 have another meaning in a different system?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: On RECEIVER, display a cross if decoded is below 1 or above 3. Explain why a wrong key can still produce a valid but incorrect message.

docs.title: Project reference 09: Classroom help system: build
docs.text:
Learning intention: Build a specified pupil-to-teacher help and acknowledgement system.

Key ideas: Requirements; design; variables; radio events

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 9: Radio communication

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Read the requirements
docs.text:
1. You will build exactly this system: pupil A sends HELP; teacher sees H; teacher B sends OK; pupil sees a tick.
  2. Complete the workbook design before coding: identify the user of each board, inputs, messages and outputs.
  3. Work in a pair with two boards. Create two NEW projects called S1-09-Pupil and S1-09-Teacher. Use lesson 7 as a reference, but name the programs clearly.
  4. Set the same teacher-allocated radio group in both on start blocks. Use a different group from other pairs.

docs.title: Task 2: Build PUPIL
docs.text:
1. On button A pressed: radio send string HELP, then show icon Question.
  2. On radio received receivedString: if receivedString = OK, show icon Yes.
  3. This first version is allowed to send repeated requests. You will fix that in lesson 10.

docs.title: Task 3: Build TEACHER with a test counter
docs.text:
1. Make a variable requests. Set requests to 0 in on start.
  2. On radio received receivedString: if receivedString = HELP, change requests by 1 and show string H.
  3. On button A pressed: show number requests. This is your diagnostic test counter. It counts requests, not different pupils.
  4. On button B pressed: radio send string OK, then clear screen.
  5. Test the request and acknowledgement. Press pupil A three times, waiting for each press to register. Teacher A should show 3 after a fresh reset.
  6. Save both projects. Record the repeated-request problem and take both code screenshots.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Reset both boards; pupil A once Pupil shows question mark; teacher shows H. Teacher A Counter shows 1. Pupil A twice more; teacher A Counter shows 3. Teacher B Pupil shows tick; teacher clears. Send unrelated string TEST using a temporary test sender Neither board treats TEST as HELP or OK.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: Complete PUPIL program, before lesson 10 changes.
  • Screenshot: Complete TEACHER program, including requests counter.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. State two requirements of this system.
  2. Why does the teacher counter not tell us the number of different pupils?
  3. What is wrong with allowing repeated HELP requests while waiting?

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: Add teacher A+B to reset requests to 0. Keep B as acknowledgement and A as viewing the count.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Save the named project and a .hex backup.
  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Project reference 10: Classroom help system: test and improve
docs.text:
Learning intention: Prevent duplicate requests, reuse a function and evaluate against requirements.

Key ideas: Boolean state; selection; subprograms; systematic testing

Time: 55 minutes.

docs.title: Related teaching pages
docs.text:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 7: Functions
  • Lesson 10: Integration, testing and evaluation

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

docs.title: Task 1: Make a separate improved version
docs.text:
1. Open each lesson 9 project and save a copy named S1-10-Pupil or S1-10-Teacher. If your editor does not offer duplicate, download a .hex backup then rename the open project.
  2. Keep the teacher counter from lesson 9. It is how you will prove duplicate requests are blocked.
  3. In the PUPIL program, create a variable waiting. In on start, set waiting to false after the radio group is set.

docs.title: Task 2: Guard the request
docs.text:
1. In PUPIL on button A pressed, wrap the existing send and icon blocks inside if NOT waiting. Find not in Logic.
  2. At the TOP of that if branch, set waiting to true. Then send HELP and show Question. Changing the state first closes the duplicate-request window.
  3. In the received OK branch, add set waiting to false before showing the tick.

docs.title: Task 3: Reuse the ready display
docs.text:
1. Make a function showReady with no extra input spaces. Inside: clear screen, then show icon SmallSquare.
  2. Call showReady at the end of on start.
  3. Add pupil on button B pressed. Inside, if NOT waiting, call showReady. B returns the idle display to ready after acknowledgement; it cannot cancel an outstanding request.
  4. The teacher program stays as lesson 9. Rename it clearly and download both programs.

docs.title: Task 4: Test and evaluate
docs.text:
1. Reset BOTH boards and wait for startup. Use the complete test table below in order.
  2. Record actual results; do not write Pass until you have performed each test.
  3. If a test fails, record the fault, change the code and repeat that test.
  4. Take final screenshots of BOTH programs, including the function. Answer the workbook questions individually even if you shared boards.
  5. Finish with two sentences: which requirements were met, and one limitation of this prototype.

docs.title: Test your program
docs.text: Test Expected result Reset both boards Pupil shows ready symbol; teacher requests is 0. Pupil A once; teacher A Pupil waiting true; question mark; teacher count 1. Pupil A three more times; teacher A Teacher count remains 1. Pupil B while waiting No cancellation; waiting remains true. Teacher B Pupil waiting false; tick appears; teacher clears. Pupil B Ready symbol returns. Pupil A again; teacher A New request works; teacher count becomes 2.

docs.title: Complete your workbook
docs.text:
• Screenshot: Final PUPIL code, including showReady and all events.
  • Screenshot: Final TEACHER code, including the requests counter.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. Explain how waiting prevents duplicate requests.
  2. Where is showReady called, and why use a function?
  3. Explain how the button event and receive event communicate through waiting.
  4. Name one real-world limitation of this prototype.

docs.title: Optional challenge
docs.text: Add a teacher-controlled recovery procedure: if a message is lost, reset BOTH boards together and test again. Explain why simply clearing waiting could create duplicate requests.

docs.title: Before you leave
docs.text:
• Save the named project and a .hex backup.
  • Paste readable screenshots into this lesson's workbook section.
  • Record actual test results and any repair.

docs.title: Teaching sequence
docs.text:
Learn one focus at a time, connect it to the micro:bit, then apply it in your workbook. Reuse and extend earlier programs where indicated.

Lesson Focus Practical application 1 Inputs, events and sequence Button-controlled character 2 Variables and random numbers Stored dice roll 3 Selection and comparisons Decisions using the dice 4 Iteration Animation and repeated sensor readings 5 Boolean logic and state Armed light alarm 6 Coordinates and boundaries Tilt-controlled dot 7 Functions Reusable game reset 8 Lists and indexing Memory sequence 9 Radio communication Classroom help-system build 10 Integration, testing and evaluation Help-system improvements and evaluation

docs.title: Using these pages
docs.text: Read the explanation, discuss the diagram, predict the example, and complete your teacher's chosen workbook task. Record actual results and explain changes. Supplied code can use supporting blocks without every detail becoming a learning objective. Functions are taught as named groups of instructions that can be defined, called and reused.

docs.title: Workbook and project references
docs.text: The Google Docs pupil workbook follows this sequence. Each lesson has three numbered tasks: Lesson 1 uses Tasks 1.1-1.3, through to Lesson 10 using Tasks 10.1-10.3. The practical guides keep their original project numbers, which differ from this teaching sequence. Links on each teaching page identify the relevant parts to use.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text: The reaction timer and secret signals are optional extension projects after the relevant concepts have been taught.

docs.title: Lesson 1: Inputs, events and sequence
docs.text: Learning intention: Identify an input and an output; explain an event; put instructions in order.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: An input supplies information. An event starts a section of instructions when something happens. Sequence is the order those instructions run. The display is an output.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Pressing A starts this event. The face appears first, stays visible during the pause, and is replaced by a heart.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on button A pressed:
    show happy face
    pause 500 ms
    show heart

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: What is the input? Which output appears first? What changes if you swap the two show blocks?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Create button reactions using a short sequence of images and pauses. Do not add a repeat or forever loop yet.

Evidence and explanation: Show your button event, identify its input and output, and explain why instruction order matters.

Complete Tasks 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Pocket personality: button events and sequences.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 2: Variables and random numbers
docs.text: Learning intention: Store a number in a variable and explain how a random range works.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: A variable is a named place to store a value. Setting it replaces its current value. A random-number block chooses a value within the limits you give it.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Shaking chooses and stores a new roll. Pressing A displays the stored value without rolling again. Set roll to 1 at startup so A also has a value before the first shake.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on shake:
    set roll to pick random 1 to 6
    show number roll
on button A pressed:
    show number roll

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: If roll stores 4, what will two A presses display? Can 0 or 7 be generated by the stated range?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Build the dice without an if block. Record 30 rolls and check every result is between 1 and 6. Keep this project for Lesson 3.

Evidence and explanation: Explain what roll stores and the difference between generating a new value and displaying the stored value.

Complete Tasks 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Dice reference: use the corrected dice in Task 2; investigate its faulty condition in Lesson 3.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 3: Selection and comparisons
docs.text: Learning intention: Use an if condition to choose whether instructions run.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: Selection makes a decision. A condition is a check with a true or false result. Equality (=) checks whether values match; > and < compare their size.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Continue with the dice from Lesson 2. Button B checks the stored roll; it does not generate another number. The else branch runs when roll is not 6.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on button B pressed:
    if roll = 6:
        show happy face
    else:
        show number roll

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: Trace the event for roll = 6 and roll = 2. Does displaying a face change the value stored in roll?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Add a decision to your existing dice. Then inspect the faulty rule that changes every 6 to 1 and explain why it makes the dice unfair.

Evidence and explanation: Include your condition, predictions for both outcomes and actual test results.

Complete Tasks 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Faulty dice investigation: trace the if rule in Task 1, then repair it.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 4: Iteration
docs.text: Learning intention: Explain counted repetition and distinguish it from continuous repetition.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: Iteration means repeating instructions. A repeat loop runs a fixed number of times. A forever loop keeps running its enclosed instructions while the program runs.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Return to the character from Lesson 1 and add the shake animation. Both show blocks and both pauses belong inside the loop. Later, try a separate forever example that repeatedly displays the light level.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on shake:
    repeat 3 times:
        show diamond
        pause 200 ms
        show small diamond
        pause 200 ms

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: How many image instructions run after one shake? How is repeat 3 different from forever?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Add and test the counted animation. In a separate example, use forever to show the light level, pause 500 ms, then repeat automatically as you cover and uncover the display.

Evidence and explanation: Show both loop structures and explain when each is useful.

Complete Tasks 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Character reference: reopen the button project, then add the shake loop shown on this teaching page.
  • Light measurement reference: the alarm is developed in Lesson 5.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 5: Boolean logic and state
docs.text: Learning intention: Use true/false values to record state and combine checks with AND.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: A Boolean value is true or false. State records the current situation of a program. AND requires both checks to be true; NOT reverses a true/false result.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Set armed and triggered to false at startup. Button A clears triggered then sets armed to true. Button B sets both to false and clears the display. Once triggered is true, covering the display does not reset it.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

forever:
    if armed AND light level > threshold:
        set triggered to true
    if armed AND triggered:
        show cross
        pause 200 ms
        clear screen
        pause 200 ms

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: Will the alarm trigger when armed is false? Why does it keep flashing after the light drops?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Measure covered and uncovered light readings. Choose a threshold between them, then build and test the armed alarm.

Evidence and explanation: Record your threshold, a test while disarmed, a trigger test and a stop test. Explain what each Boolean variable records.

Complete Tasks 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Use the alarm build instructions and test table.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 6: Coordinates and boundaries
docs.text: Learning intention: Use display coordinates and conditions to keep a moving dot within the screen.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: The display has five rows and five columns. Coordinates run from 0 to 4. x increases to the right; y increases downwards. Boundary checks stop a position leaving that range.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: The player stays on row 4 while x changes. Start with this moving dot; scoring and reset routines can be added later.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on start:
    set x to 2
forever:
    if acceleration x < -300 AND x > 0:
        change x by -1
    if acceleration x > 300 AND x < 4:
        change x by 1
    clear screen
    plot x, 4
    pause 200 ms

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: At x = 0, what happens on a left tilt? Where is the point 2, 4?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Build the moving dot and test both edges repeatedly. Reuse your conditions, loop and variable knowledge.

Evidence and explanation: Label the axes, explain one boundary condition and record the results at both edges.

Complete Tasks 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Use the movement and boundary examples. Leave resetGame until Lesson 7.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 7: Functions
docs.text: Learning intention: Define a named group of instructions, call it and explain why reuse is useful.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: A function groups instructions under a name. Defining it specifies what it does. Calling it runs those instructions. The same function can be called from different places.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Continue the tilt project. Put the reset instructions in one function and call it at startup and from button A. If both places need the same reset behaviour, you only need to edit the function once.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

function resetGame:
    set x to 2
    set score to 0
    clear screen
on start:
    call resetGame
on button A pressed:
    call resetGame

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: Does defining resetGame run it? Where is it called? What changes at both call sites if you add an instruction inside it?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Create resetGame, move your reset instructions inside it and call it from startup and button A. Use a name that describes its purpose.

Evidence and explanation: Show the function and its two calls. Explain the difference between defining and calling it.

Complete Tasks 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Use the resetGame example; extend the reset instructions if you add the target and score.
  • Later reuse: showReady is another named group of instructions.

Focus on this lesson

Follow the instructions for any supplied blocks. You only need to explain the concepts in this lesson; extra spaces and labels in supplied function blocks are not additional vocabulary to learn.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 8: Lists and indexing
docs.text: Learning intention: Read values from an ordered list using their positions.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: A list stores an ordered collection of values. An index identifies a position. The first item has index 0. List length is the number of items.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Use the supplied memory-game framework to play and check a sequence. Here 0 represents A and 1 represents B. The example is the correct-answer part of the checker; the framework also handles wrong answers and playback.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

set sequence to [0, 1, 0]
set position to 0
if choice = sequence[position]:
    change position by 1
    if position = length of sequence:
        set accepting to false
        show tick

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: What is stored at index 1 in [0, 1, 0]? For a list of four items, what are the valid indexes?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Complete the checker using the supplied framework. In the A event, use the supplied checkChoice call with 0 in its space; in B, put 1 in its space. Keep those supplied blocks and focus on the list and its positions.

Evidence and explanation: Record tests for both sequence lengths. Explain why checking list length works better than always checking for 3.

Complete Tasks 8.1, 8.2 and 8.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Use the list setup, checking instructions and test table.

Focus on this lesson

Follow the instructions for any supplied blocks. You only need to explain the concepts in this lesson; extra spaces and labels in supplied function blocks are not additional vocabulary to learn.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 9: Radio communication
docs.text: Learning intention: Send and receive agreed messages between two micro:bits.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: Radio lets micro:bits exchange messages. Both programs need the same allocated radio group and must agree what each message means. A receive event starts when a message arrives.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Pupil A sends HELP. Teacher B sends OK. The pupil displays a tick when OK arrives. Text must match exactly, including capitals. The counter records requests, not different pupils.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on radio received receivedString:
    if receivedString = "HELP":
        change requests by 1
        show string "H"

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: Which event sends HELP? Which event handles it? Why can two boards with different groups fail to communicate?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Build the pupil and teacher help programs. Test the request, acknowledgement and repeated requests. Save them for Lesson 10.

Evidence and explanation: Draw the message journey, include both programs and record what happens after repeated A presses.

Complete Tasks 9.1, 9.2 and 9.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

docs.title: Practical references
docs.text:
These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Use the two-board help-system build and its request counter.
  • Additional reference for sending and receiving HELP and OK.

Back to the teaching sequence

docs.title: Lesson 10: Integration, testing and evaluation
docs.text: Learning intention: Combine earlier concepts, prevent duplicate requests and evaluate against requirements.

docs.title: Understand the concept
docs.text: A requirement says what the system must do. A useful test has an action, an expected result and an actual result. Debugging finds and repairs faults; evaluation uses evidence to judge how well requirements were met.

docs.title: Connect it to the micro:bit
docs.text: Set waiting to false at startup. Setting it true before sending closes the opportunity for another request while waiting. Keep the teacher counter so you can prove that repeated presses do not send duplicates.

docs.title: Read the example
docs.text:
This is pseudocode showing the order and structure of the MakeCode Blocks. It is not code to paste into the editor.

on button A pressed:
    if NOT waiting:
        set waiting to true
        radio send string "HELP"
        show question mark
on radio received receivedString:
    if receivedString = "OK":
        set waiting to false
        show tick

docs.title: Predict and discuss
docs.text: After one request and three more A presses, what should the teacher count show? What must happen before another request is allowed?

docs.title: Apply it in your workbook
docs.text:
Improve the Lesson 9 programs, reuse showReady and run the full test table. Record faults and retests.

Evidence and explanation: Include expected and actual results, both final programs, a repair if needed, and an evaluation naming one limitation.

Complete Tasks 10.1, 10.2 and 10.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.
